{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=continuous+attractor+dynamics+preference+stability+path+dependence&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7540068\", \"title\": [\"Attractor-Weighted Neuromodulation of Reward Path Dependence and Habit Formation\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>This paper proposes a formal dynamical-systems theory of reward-seeking path dependence in the brain. The central claim is that repeated reward-seeking does not merely increase or decrease dopamine in a colloquial sense; rather, it reshapes a multiscale state space in which action sequences become attractors, habit chunks, and context-sensitive policy priors. The model is built on three established empirical commitments: first, midbrain dopamine neurons encode reward prediction error rather than pleasure itself; second, dopamine contributes more to wanting than liking ; and third, cortico-striatal circuits progressively chunk repeated actions into stable habit-like sequences. We extend these findings into a multineuromodulator model in which dopamine, opioids, serotonin, noradrenaline, and acetylcholine jointly regulate incentive salience, hedonic impact, temporal discounting, and uncertainty. The resulting theory explains why some reward paths intensify into compulsive attractors, why devaluation does not automatically terminate them, and why transitions to alternative behavioral regimes depend on a stability shift in the underlying attractor landscape rather than on a simple drop in reward.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7540068\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.14711/thesis-b1114789\", \"title\": [\"Dynamics of continuous attractor neural networks\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.14711/thesis-b1114789\"}, {\"DOI\": \"10.14711/thesis-b1252000\", \"title\": [\"Dynamics of continuous attractor neural networks with dynamical synapses\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.14711/thesis-b1252000\"}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2202/1558-3708.1104\", \"title\": [\"Stochastic Growth with Increasing Returns: Stability and Path Dependence\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2202/1558-3708.1104\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2003, 1, 1]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "d562f2a49aef7899940…

is a novel Koopman -based technique that effectively dissects high -dimensional 
nonlinear systems into periodically distinct constituents on reduced -order

with an engineering-oriented emphasis. It aimed at elucidating how sampling range

shear flow over a prism —for optimal pertinency. We numerically simulated the 
flow by the dynamic -stress Large-Eddies Simulation with Near -Wall Resolution.

summary: This study investigates the dynamics of a magnetic pendulum under time-varying magnetic excitation with a position-dependent phase. The system exhibits complex chaotic and regular dynamics, validated through simulations and experiments. The mathematical model, based on a physical setup, includes a magnetic excitation torque with phase dependence on the dynamic variable. Bifurcation analyses confirm the rich multistability of the system, showcasing periodic attractors, period-doubling bifurcations, and chaotic behavior. Experimental validation demonstrates a high agreement between numerical and experimental results, supporting the efficacy of the proposed model. The study sheds light on the system's sensitivity to changes in magnetic interaction, providing insights into controlling resonance energy exchange in coupled magnetic pendulum systems.

Data-driven surrogate models using artificial neural networks have been proposed as an efficient alternative to numerical modeling, where Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are increasingly being used for path-dependent multiscale modeling. In this study, we perform a systematic comparison between RNNs and transformer models trained on sequences of homogenized response of SFRC. We study the effect on two types of hyperparameters, namely architectural hyperparameters (such as the number of GRU layers, hidden size, number of attention heads, and encoder blocks) and training hyperparameters (such as learning rate and batch size).
